To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk. Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/respiratory-syncytial-virus-rsv-maternal-vaccination-coverage-in-england/respiratory-syncytial-virus-rsv-maternal-vaccination-coverage-in-england-february-2026-report Published 2 July 2026 This report presents monthly vaccine uptake data for the maternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunisation programme in England, focusing on the period up to February 2026. This report includes vaccine uptake estimates for pregnant women who delivered in the 18th month of the maternal vaccination programme in February 2026. Main points The main messages of this report are: 62.5% (23,691 out of 37,884) of women that reported giving birth during the survey month received an RSV vaccine uptake varied by NHS commissioning region, with the highest uptake reported in the South West region (72.4%) and the lowest in the London region (52.1%) uptake varied across integrated care boards (ICBs) with the highest uptake reported in the Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly ICB (79.9%) and the lowest in Birmingham and Solihull (40.1%) uptake varied across local authorities with the highest uptake reported in the Isle of Wight (87.3%) and the lowest in Enfield (33.5%) uptake varied by ethnic group, with the highest uptake reported among the Asian or Asian British - Chinese ethnic group (76.8%) and the lowest among the Black - Caribbean ethnic group (40.1%) Help us improve this resource This vaccine uptake report has been designated as an Official Statistics release. As part of this process, we are seeking feedback from users to ensure the publication meets your needs. We would be grateful if you could take a few minutes to complete a short survey and share your views. Please complete the survey Your input will play an important role in shaping the development of this publication. Thank you for your time and support. Analysis of maternal RSV vaccine uptake Maternal uptake of the RSV vaccine is assessed monthly to monitor the reach and impact of the national immunisation programme. Given the programme’s design, uptake is defined as the proportion of pregnant women who delivered in the reporting month and had received the RSV vaccine during pregnancy. This metric serves as a proxy for vaccine coverage by infant birth month, reflecting the extent of passive immunity conferred to newborns. This monthly report presents RSV vaccine uptake for women who delivered in the eighteenth month of the RSV vaccination programme in February 2026. The monthly uptake trend among pregnant women who have delivered since the programme’s launch is presented in Figure 1. Overall, the monthly RSV maternal vaccine uptake for February 2026 was 62.5%. RSV uptake increased in the first few months of the programme and has remained steady since October 2025. Figure 1. RSV vaccine uptake (%) trend among pregnant women by month of delivery, measured in February 2026 Note 1: the vertical lines represent a change in the percentage of GP (general practitioner) practices used to calculate RSV vaccine uptake. Up to December 2024, vaccine uptake was estimated based on data from a single supplier covering fewer than 40.5% of GP practices. From January 2025 onwards, vaccine uptake was based on data from more than 97.5% of GP practices and is more representative of national vaccination uptake. This month’s report includes data from both major GP IT suppliers, significantly expanding the data available in earliest reports (September to December 2024). It includes data from 99% of GPs in England, up from 40.4% of participating GPs previously in the first 4 months (September to December 2024) of the vaccination programme. This has been made possible by improvements in data quality and permits a more representative analysis of uptake and trends across England. To further explore variation in uptake, Table 1 presents uptake by commissioning region, while Table 2 provides the breakdown by ethnicity. As shown in Table 1, there are notable regional differences in uptake, with variation of up to 20.3 percentage points between NHS commissioning regions. Table 1. RSV vaccine uptake (%) in pregnant women, measured in February 2026, by NHS commissioning region Change to table view Commissioning region RSV uptake (%) North East and Yorkshire 64.0 North West 61.4 Midlands 59.2 East of England 65.4 London 52.1 South East 70.0 South West 72.4 Commissioning region RSV uptake (%) North East and Yorkshire 64.0 North West 61.4 Midlands 59.2 East of England 65.4 London 52.1 South East 70.0 South West 72.4 Variation in uptake by ethnicity was also observed, with a gap of 36.7 percentage points observed in the uptake between ethnic groups (Table 2). Table 2. RSV vaccine uptake (%) in pregnant women, measured in February 2026, by ethnicity Change to table view Ethnic group [note 2] RSV uptake (%) Asian or Asian British - any other Asian background 62.7 Asian or Asian British - Bangladeshi 51.4 Asian or Asian British - Chinese 76.8 Asian or Asian British - Indian 70.2 Asian or Asian British - Pakistani 46.3 Black or Black British - African 47.1 Black or Black British - any other Black background 48.3 Black or Black British - Caribbean 40.1 Mixed - any other mixed background 54.3 Mixed - White and Asian 60.7 Mixed - White and Black African 54.2 Mixed - White and Black Caribbean 47.5 White - British 70.1 White - Irish 66.2 White - any other White background 48.2 Any other ethnicity code 62.1 Ethnicity - unknown 57.4 Other ethnic group - any other ethnic group 50.2 Ethnic group [note 2] RSV uptake (%) Asian or Asian British - any other Asian background 62.7 Asian or Asian British - Bangladeshi 51.4 Asian or Asian British - Chinese 76.8 Asian or Asian British - Indian 70.2 Asian or Asian British - Pakistani 46.3 Black or Black British - African 47.1 Black or Black British - any other Black background 48.3 Black or Black British - Caribbean 40.1 Mixed - any other mixed background 54.3 Mixed - White and Asian 60.7 Mixed - White and Black African 54.2 Mixed - White and Black Caribbean 47.5 White - British 70.1 White - Irish 66.2 White - any other White background 48.2 Any other ethnicity code 62.1 Ethnicity - unknown 57.4 Other ethnic group - any other ethnic group 50.2 Note 2: the ‘Ethnicity - unknown’ group combines all records where ethnicity was not provided. This includes people whose ethnicity was not recorded, not stated, or who refused to give their ethnicity. The ‘any other ethnicity code’ category includes individuals whose ethnicity has been recorded using non-standard or legacy codes (that is, codes not aligned with the 2001 or 2011 Census classifications). The map in Figure 2 shows RSV uptake by ICB. Uptake varied across ICBs by 39.8 percentage points with the highest uptake reported in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly (79.9) and the lowest uptake reported in Birmingham and Solihull (40.1). Figure 2. RSV vaccine uptake (%) among pregnant women delivering in February 2026, by ICBs Across the local authorities, uptake differed by 53.8 percentage points with the highest uptake reported in Isle of Wight (87.3%) and the lowest uptake reported in Enfield (33.5%). The variation across local authorities is presented in the map shown in Figure 3. Figure 3. RSV vaccine uptake (%) among pregnant women delivering in February 2026, by local authority Further detail, including uptake figures broken down by local authority and ICB, can be found in the February 2026 data tables. Since the RSV maternal vaccination programme has now been running for eighteen months (up to the reporting month), an increasing number of pregnant women are receiving the vaccine during their eligible window. This growing awareness and notification from gestation week 20 onwards have contributed to a gradual increase in monthly vaccine uptake from 40.5% in September 2024 to the current figure reported for February 2026. As the programme continues and more women are informed earlier in their pregnancies, monthly vaccination uptake is expected to gradually increase. Data sources and methodology More information is available in our quality and methodology information (QMI) report. The maternal RSV vaccination report will be released monthly, presenting vaccination uptake data only for the specific reporting month, without cumulative figures from previous months. The reporting period for the current report is from 1 February 2026 to 28 February 2026. This report focuses on pregnant women who delivered in the survey month, regardless of gestational age at birth. GP-level RSV vaccine uptake data is automatically uploaded via participating GP IT suppliers to the ImmForm website each month. ImmForm data is validated and analysed by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) to check data completeness, query any anomalous data and describe epidemiological trends. Since September 2024, the reporting data collected includes: denominator: number of women who delivered in the survey month, excluding miscarriages and stillbirths, regardless of gestational age numerator: number of women receiving RSV vaccination from week 28 of pregnancy up until delivery refusals: number of women in the denominator who refused RSV vaccination between week 28 of pregnancy and delivery To ensure accurate denominators are extracted from GP IT systems by the automated survey and precise uptake estimates are calculated, the methodology uses a monthly data extraction process with a three-month reporting lag to allow enough time for relevant information to be recorded. For example, data from September 2024 was extracted on 1 December, 2024. The data presented in this report for February 2026 is based on data received from both major GP IT suppliers, accounting for 99% of all national GP practices participating during the reporting month. The March 2026 maternal RSV vaccination uptake report is scheduled to be released on 6 August 2026. Background information The RSV vaccine has been offered to pregnant women in England since September 2024 to address the significant burden of RSV-related illness, hospitalisations and deaths, particularly among infants under six months of age and older adults, who are at increased risk of lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) (see the Green Book on immunisation). In 2023, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) issued a full statement recommending the implementation of a maternal RSV vaccination programme. This recommendation was based on robust evidence demonstrating the safety and effectiveness of RSV vaccines in protecting infants during their most vulnerable period. The vaccine is recommended as a year-round programme to be administered from 28 weeks of gestation onwards. This timing aligns with the optimal window for passive antibody transfer to the foetus, ensuring effective protection against severe RSV-related illness. From 1 September 2024 (the programme start date), all women who are at least 28 weeks pregnant are advised to receive the vaccine as soon as possible, with vaccination continuing to be recommended for all eligible women throughout pregnancy up until delivery. Additionally, the vaccine will be reoffered for every subsequent pregnancy to maintain consistent coverage and protection. This monthly report includes vaccine uptake data for women who delivered in February 2026. Programme delivery The programme is delivered through GP and maternity services, ensuring accessible vaccination opportunities for eligible pregnant women across England. In addition, the RSV vaccine is available through the community pharmacy delivery model at approximately 37 sites across 2 ICBs in the East of England. It is also available at up to 200 additional community pharmacy sites across the Midlands, North West, and London commissioning regions during the 2025 to 2026 expansion phase. Previous monthly reports are available at RSV maternal vaccination coverage in England. analysis.time: Published 2 July 2026; event date is February 2026; the report covers data up to February 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: England, focusing on pregnant women who delivered in the 18th month of the RSV vaccination programme, with data broken down by NHS commissioning regions, integrated care boards (ICBs), and local authorities.
analysis.event: A report on the maternal RSV vaccination coverage in England, published by the UK Health Security Agency, detailing the uptake of the RSV vaccine among pregnant women who delivered in February 2026. The report is an official statistics release.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The RSV vaccine uptake was 62.5% (23,691 out of 37,884) among women who delivered in February 2026. Uptake varied significantly by region, with the highest in the South West (72.4%) and the lowest in London (52.1%). It also varied by ICB, with Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly (79.9%) having the highest and Birmingham and Solihull (40.1%) the lowest. Uptake varied by ethnicity, with a gap of 36.7 percentage points observed between ethnic groups.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: It includes analysis of uptake by region, ICB, and ethnicity, and is part of the national immunisation programme aimed at reducing RSV-related illness, hospitalisations, and deaths in infants under six months of age and older adults.

analysis.brief_en: This report, published by the UK Health Security Agency on 2 July 2026, details the maternal RSV vaccination coverage in England as of February 2026. It states that 62.5% of pregnant women who delivered in February 2026 received the RSV vaccine, with regional variations observed, such as the South West region reporting the highest uptake at 72.4% and London the lowest at 52.1%. Integrated care boards (ICBs) also showed significant differences, with Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly at 79.9% and Birmingham and Solihull at 40.1%. Ethnicity-based variations were noted, with a 36.7 percentage point gap between groups. The data is based on improved quality and covers over 97.5% of GP practices since January 2025. The programme aims to reduce RSV-related illness, hospitalisations, and deaths in vulnerable populations, including infants under six months and older adults.

news.content_zh: 这份报告由英国健康安全局于 2026 年 7 月 2 日发布,详细介绍了截至 2026 年 2 月英国孕产妇 RSV 疫苗 覆盖率。报告指出,2026 年 2 月分娩的孕妇中有 62.5% 接种了 RSV 疫苗,但存在地区差异,例如西南地区报告的接种率最高,为 72.4%,伦敦最低,为 52.1%。综合护理委员会 (ICB) 也显示出显着差异,康沃尔郡和锡利群岛为 79.9%,伯明翰和索利哈尔为 40.1%。注意到基于种族的差异,各组之间存在 36.7 个百分点的差距。该数据基于改进的质量,涵盖自 2025 年 1 月以来超过 97.5% 的全科医生诊所。该计划旨在减少弱势群体(包括六个月以下的婴儿和老年人)与 RSV 相关的疾病、住院和死亡。

She joined Britannica in 2006 and... Kara Rogers Fact-checked by Britannica Editors Encyclopaedia Britannica's editors oversee subject areas in which they have extensive knowledge, whether from years of experience gained by working on that content or via study for an advanced degree.... Britannica Editors Last updated Sep. 6, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything News • Medical groups offer vaccine guidance to fill federal vacuum • Sep. 2, 2026, 10:00 AM ET (NPR) ...(Show more) Hong Kong teen’s will to fight illness ‘incredibly low’ after near-death scares • Aug. 14, 2026, 4:12 AM ET (South China Morning Post) Show less respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infectious agent of the respiratory system that typically produces a mild coldlike illness but in susceptible individuals, particularly infants under six months of age, is a major cause of severe and potentially fatal lower respiratory disease. Severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) occurs most commonly in the elderly and in young children. An estimated 60 to 70 percent of children have been infected with RSV by age one, and nearly all children have been infected by age two. Because RSV effectively evades immunity, repeat infections are common. RSV infection is seasonal, occurring as an annual epidemic during the winter in most countries in temperate regions. What's the Difference Between Bacteria and Viruses?Knowing the difference isn't just a technical distinction—it can save lives.(more) See all videos for this article Direct person-to-person contact is thought to be the most common route of RSV transmission. The virus also can be transmitted through the air, such as by coughing or sneezing, and through direct contact with a contaminated surface followed by touching of the face. Symptoms generally appear within four to six days of infection and include runny nose, cough, sore throat, headache, fever, and wheezing. In instances of severe illness, affected individuals may have a high fever, severe wheezing, rapid or laboured breathing, and bluish lips or fingers. Infants may only show signs of irritability, fatigue, and breathing difficulties, even in severe cases. The only pharmacological therapy available for treatment of RSV is the nucleoside analogue ribavirin, which can be administered orally, parenterally (by injection or infusion), or by inhalation. An injectable humanized monoclonal antibody is available for prevention of severe RSV illness in high-risk infants and children. It provides passive immunity and must by given by intramuscular injection once a month during RSV season. Transmission can be prevented with frequent handwashing, cleaning of surfaces, avoiding close contact with others, and covering the mouth and nose with the upper arm when coughing or sneezing. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Quick Summary Table of Contents Table of Contents Quick Summary Ask Anything Top Questions What is a respiratory disease? Respiratory diseases are diseases and disorders that impact the airways and lungs, affecting human respiration. These diseases can affect any part of the respiratory system, including the nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, lung tissues, and respiratory muscles of the chest cage. The respiratory tract is susceptible to a wide range of disorders because it is exposed to the environment, has a large network of capillaries, and can be the site of allergic reactions. Common respiratory diseases in children include the common cold, tonsillitis, croup, allergic rhinitis, and asthma. 3 Britannica Sources childhood disease and disorder: Respiratory disorders respiratory disease therapeutics: The respiratory system This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Which parts of the body are affected by respiratory diseases? Respiratory diseases can affect any structure or organ involved in breathing. This includes the nasal cavities, pharynx (or throat), larynx, trachea (or windpipe), bronchi and bronchioles, the tissues of the lungs, and the respiratory muscles of the chest cage. Additionally, the pleura, the protective membrane covering the lungs, and the diaphragm can be affected by respiratory disease. 3 Britannica Sources infectious disease: Chlamydial organisms respiratory disease human respiratory system: The intrapulmonary conducting airways: bronchi and bronchioles This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What are some common types of respiratory diseases? Respiratory diseases affect the organs and structures involved in breathing, including the lungs, nasal cavities, and bronchi. Common types of respiratory diseases: * Infections Common infections include the common cold, influenza, pneumonia, bronchitis, tonsillitis, sinusitis, and croup. Lower respiratory tract infections are especially dangerous for young children, older people, and individuals with weakened immune systems. * Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) COPD includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis, which damage the airways and reduce airflow in and out of the lungs. The leading cause of COPD is long-term exposure to tobacco smoke. * Allergic Disorders Asthma and allergic rhinitis are common allergic disorders that cause inflammation and obstruction of the respiratory tract. * Other Lung Conditions Other conditions include tuberculosis and cystic fibrosis, which predominantly affect the lungs but may involve other organs. 4 Britannica Sources List of Deadliest Diseases: Lower respiratory tract infection childhood disease and disorder: Respiratory disorders respiratory disease: Viral infections of the respiratory system therapeutics: The respiratory system This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How can respiratory diseases spread from one person to another? Respiratory diseases spread through various routes. Common methods include airborne transmission via respiratory droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Close proximity to a contagious individual increases the risk of inhaling these droplets. Infection can also occur through direct contact with contaminated surfaces. If a person touches a surface with the virus and then touches their mouth, nose, or eyes, transmission may occur. Additionally, dust particles containing infectious agents can cause disease if they come into contact with food, skin, or are inhaled into the respiratory system. 6 Britannica Sources List of Deadliest Diseases: Lower respiratory tract infection infectious disease: The inanimate environment Questions About COVID-19 Answered: How is COVID-19 transmitted? Definition of respiratory syncytial virus infection: Transmission COVID-19 in 20 Questions: How does the disease spread? This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What symptoms might someone with a respiratory disease have? Symptoms of respiratory disease can include a cough, which may or may not produce sputum. The presence of blood in the sputum, known as hemoptysis, should always be checked by a medical professional. Another common symptom is dyspnea, or shortness of breath, which can arise suddenly or develop slowly over time. Chest pain may also occur, especially with pneumonia, and is typically felt when taking a deep breath. Wheezing in the chest may be heard due to narrowed airways. Other indicators include swelling of the fingertips, known as clubbing, and enlarged lymph nodes. General symptoms such as fatigue, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss can also indicate a respiratory illness. 3 Britannica Sources childhood disease and disorder: Respiratory disorders Synonyms of wheezing respiratory disease: Signs and symptoms This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How can people prevent or manage respiratory diseases? To prevent or manage respiratory diseases, minimize exposure to triggers, such as allergens and pollutants, and maintain good hygiene through frequent handwashing. Avoid smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke, as these are major risk factors for respiratory illnesses like COPD and lung cancer. Britannica Editors Last updated Sep. 6, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything News • Medical groups offer vaccine guidance to fill federal vacuum • Sep. 2, 2026, 10:00 AM ET (NPR) ...(Show more) Hong Kong teen’s will to fight illness ‘incredibly low’ after near-death scares • Aug. 14, 2026, 4:12 AM ET (South China Morning Post) Show less respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infectious agent of the respiratory system that typically produces a mild coldlike illness but in susceptible individuals, particularly infants under six months of age, is a major cause of severe and potentially fatal lower respiratory disease. Severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) occurs most commonly in the elderly and in young children. An estimated 60 to 70 percent of children have been infected with RSV by age one, and nearly all children have been infected by age two. Because RSV effectively evades immunity, repeat infections are common. RSV infection is seasonal, occurring as an annual epidemic during the winter in most countries in temperate regions. What's the Difference Between Bacteria and Viruses?Knowing the difference isn't just a technical distinction—it can save lives.(more) See all videos for this article Direct person-to-person contact is thought to be the most common route of RSV transmission. The virus also can be transmitted through the air, such as by coughing or sneezing, and through direct contact with a contaminated surface followed by touching of the face. Symptoms generally appear within four to six days of infection and include runny nose, cough, sore throat, headache, fever, and wheezing. In instances of severe illness, affected individuals may have a high fever, severe wheezing, rapid or laboured breathing, and bluish lips or fingers. Infants may only show signs of irritability, fatigue, and breathing difficulties, even in severe cases. The only pharmacological therapy available for treatment of RSV is the nucleoside analogue ribavirin, which can be administered orally, parenterally (by injection or infusion), or by inhalation. An injectable humanized monoclonal antibody is available for prevention of severe RSV illness in high-risk infants and children. It provides passive immunity and must by given by intramuscular injection once a month during RSV season. Transmission can be prevented with frequent handwashing, cleaning of surfaces, avoiding close contact with others, and covering the mouth and nose with the upper arm when coughing or sneezing. Sanofi and Keke Palmer team up to urge parents to help protect babies from serious RSV with BEYFORTUS® PR Newswire Tue, September 8, 2026 at 8:00 AM EDT 10 min read SNY Emmy Award-winning actress, entrepreneur and mom Keke Palmer partners with Sanofi to help educate families about protection against a serious respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lung infection BEYFORTUS has been chosen by millions of parents to help protect their babies from serious RSV lung infection, a leading cause of hospitalization among babies under 1 year of age Campaign encourages parents to talk to their baby's doctor about helping protect their baby against serious RSV lung infection with BEYFORTUS, the #1 prescribed RSV immunization for babies MORRISTOWN, N.J., Sept. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sanofi is partnering with Emmy Award-winning actress, entrepreneur and mom Keke Palmer to help educate families about the importance of protection against serious RSV lung infection for babies. After she discussed the risks of RSV with her son's doctor, Palmer's baby received BEYFORTUS® (nirsevimab-alip), a monoclonal antibody approved to help prevent serious RSV lung infection in newborns and infants entering their first RSV season, as well as in children up to 24 months of age who remain at risk for severe RSV through their second season. "As moms, we spend so much time preparing for our baby's arrival and thinking about how to help keep them healthy. That includes being aware of RSV and the risk it can pose during a baby's first year of life," said Keke Palmer. "When I spoke with my son's pediatrician, we discussed options for serious RSV protection, and together we decided that BEYFORTUS was right for him. That's why I'm partnering with Sanofi to encourage parents to learn more about RSV and talk with their baby's doctor about a protection plan that works for their family. For my baby that included BEYFORTUS." Palmer's message comes as families prepare for RSV season. RSV is a common and highly contagious virus that can affect any baby. While it often causes mild, cold-like symptoms, it can sometimes lead to serious respiratory illness and remains a leading cause of hospitalization among infants younger than one year of age in the United States. More than half of babies will get RSV before their first birthday. For babies entering their first RSV season, which typically runs from fall through spring in most parts of the United States, planning ahead is important. Parents of older babies who are entering their first RSV season should talk to their baby's doctor now about RSV prevention so they can avoid missing their opportunity for immunization this season. Babies born during RSV season may receive BEYFORTUS at birth or at an early well-child visit. Story Continues "Our ambition is all infant protection, all season," said Ayman Chit, Head of North America Medical, Vaccines at Sanofi. "RSV is unpredictable, and it's difficult to know which babies may become seriously ill, that's why it's important for parents to have conversations with their baby's doctor about RSV protection before or during the RSV season. BEYFORTUS delivers ready-made antibodies, helping to provide rapid protection against serious RSV lung infection for 5 months, the typical length of an RSV season. More than 11 million parents in the US have chosen BEYFORTUS for their baby, and by partnering with Keke Palmer, we're encouraging more families to learn about RSV prevention and talk with their baby's doctor about BEYFORTUS." To learn more about BEYFORTUS and serious RSV lung infection prevention, visit BEYFORTUS.com. Parents are encouraged to talk with their baby's doctor to understand if BEYFORTUS is right for their child. Keke Palmer is a paid spokesperson for Sanofi. About RSV RSV is a highly contagious virus that can lead to serious respiratory illness for infants. More than half of babies will get RSV before their first birthday. Most of the time RSV will cause a mild, cold-like illness. However, RSV is the most common cause of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD), including bronchiolitis and pneumonia, in infants. RSV LRTD is a leading cause of hospitalization in babies under 1, with most hospitalizations for RSV occurring in healthy infants born at term. Historically in the US, an estimated 590,000 RSV cases in babies under 1 have required medical care, including physician office, urgent care, emergency room visits and hospitalizations. About BEYFORTUS BEYFORTUS is a single-dose long-acting antibody designed to help prevent RSV LRTD in infants that extends through five months, the length of the typical RSV season in the US. For children undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, an additional dose of BEYFORTUS is recommended as soon as the child is stable after surgery. An additional dose of BEYFORTUS is also indicated for children up to 24 months of age, regardless of body weight, who remain vulnerable to severe RSV disease through their second RSV season. As a long-acting antibody provided directly to newborns and infants as a single dose, BEYFORTUS offers fast-acting protection to help prevent lower respiratory tract disease caused by RSV without requiring activation of the immune system. It has demonstrated a consistent safety profile across a broad infant population. BEYFORTUS administration can be timed to coincide with the RSV season. BEYFORTUS has been approved for use in the US, the European Union, China, Japan, and many other countries around the world. Special designations to facilitate expedited development of BEYFORTUS were granted by several regulatory agencies, including Breakthrough Therapy Designation and Fast Track Designation from the US Food and Drug Administration; Breakthrough Therapy Designation and Priority Review designation by The China Center for Drug Evaluation under the National Medical Products Administration; access granted to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) Priority Medicines scheme and EMA accelerated assessment; Promising Innovative Medicine designation by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency; and BEYFORTUS has been named "a medicine for prioritized development" under the Project for Drug Selection to Promote New Drug Development in Pediatrics by the Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development. INDICATION BEYFORTUS is a prescription medicine used to help prevent a serious lung disease caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in: Newborns and babies under 1 year of age born during or entering their first RSV season. Children up to 24 months of age who remain at risk of severe RSV disease through their second RSV season. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION Your child should not take BEYFORTUS if your child has a history of serious allergic reactions to nirsevimab-alip or any of the ingredients in BEYFORTUS. Before your child receives BEYFORTUS, tell your healthcare provider about all of your child's medical conditions, including if your child: has ever had a reaction to BEYFORTUS. has bleeding or bruising problems. If your child has a problem with bleeding or bruises easily, an injection could cause a problem. Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines your child takes, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. Your infant should not receive a medicine called palivizumab if they have already received BEYFORTUS in the same RSV season. Serious allergic reactions have happened with BEYFORTUS. Get medical help right away if your child has any of the following signs or symptoms of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, mouth, or tongue difficulty swallowing or breathing unresponsiveness bluish color of skin, lips, or under fingernails muscle weakness severe rash, hives, or itching The most common side effects of BEYFORTUS include rash and pain, swelling, or hardness at the site of your child's injection. These are not all the possible side effects of BEYFORTUS. Call your healthcare provider if you have questions about side effects. Please see full Prescribing Information, including Patient Information, for more details. Please see full Prescribing Information, including Patient Information, for more details. analysis.brief_en: Sanofi and Keke Palmer have launched a public health campaign to educate parents about protecting their babies from serious respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections. The initiative, which includes a partnership with the actress and entrepreneur, promotes the use of BEYFORTUS® (nirsevimab-alip), a monoclonal antibody approved to prevent severe RSV lung infections in newborns and infants up to 24 months of age. RSV is a highly contagious virus that can lead to serious respiratory illness, particularly among infants under one year old, and is a leading cause of hospitalization in this age group in the United States. The campaign emphasizes the importance of discussing RSV prevention with a baby's doctor before or during the RSV season, which typically runs from fall through spring. BEYFORTUS provides rapid protection for five months, the typical duration of an RSV season. The initiative is part of broader efforts to raise awareness about RSV and its risks, with the goal of encouraging proactive measures to safeguard infants. The campaign is not an outbreak investigation but a preventive health promotion.

Evidence showed lower hospitalization and severe illness rates following vaccination. Recommendations cover influenza, COVID-19, and RSV prevention for the 2026–2027 season. NEW respiratory virus vaccine recommendations align physician groups on protection against influenza, COVID-19, and RSV. Respiratory Virus Vaccines Address a Substantial Disease Burden Four leading U.S. physician organizations have issued recommendations for the 2026–2027 respiratory virus season, covering patients from infancy through older adulthood, as well as pregnant and immunocompromised populations. The guidance followed structured reviews of vaccine safety, effectiveness, and epidemiology. Researchers examined 69 influenza studies, 155 COVID-19 studies, and 75 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) studies published between August 2025 and June 2026. More than a dozen randomized controlled trials were included for each pathogen. The recommendations arrive as respiratory viruses continue to cause substantial morbidity and mortality. During the 2025–2026 season, influenza was associated with at least 390,000 hospitalizations and 24,000 deaths. RSV caused an estimated 170,000 to 340,000 hospitalizations, while COVID-19 was linked to between 140,000 and 250,000 hospitalizations. Evidence Supports Protection Against Severe Illness Influenza vaccination reduced hospitalization risk by 31% among adults aged 65 years or older. Vaccination during pregnancy reduced symptomatic influenza among infants younger than 6 months by 44%, while pediatric influenza vaccination was associated with an 80% reduction in deaths across eight seasons. COVID-19 vaccination reduced hospitalization risk by 53% among adults aged 65 years or older. Among people with immunocompromising conditions, vaccination lowered the risk of intensive care admission or death by 32% to 53%. Vaccination during pregnancy also reduced emergency department or urgent care visits by 58%. RSV vaccines were 69% to 83% effective against hospitalization among adults aged 60 years or older. Maternal RSV vaccination reduced RSV risk by 82%, while infant immunization with nirsevimab lowered hospitalization risk by 64% to 93%. No new safety concerns were identified across the three evidence reviews. Respiratory Virus Vaccine Recommendations by Population The guidance supports annual influenza vaccination for everyone aged 6 months or older. COVID-19 vaccination recommendations vary by age and clinical status, with particular emphasis on older adults, young children, pregnant patients, healthcare personnel, and people with compromised immune systems. RSV vaccination is recommended for adults aged 50 to 74 years with high risk conditions and all adults aged 75 years or older. Preventive options for infants include maternal RSV vaccination or nirsevimab, depending on eligibility and maternal vaccination history. For clinicians, the recommendations provide an evidence based framework for vaccine counseling and shared decision making ahead of the respiratory virus season. Reference O’Reilly KB. Evidence showed lower hospitalization and severe illness rates following vaccination. Recommendations cover influenza, COVID-19, and RSV prevention for the 2026–2027 season. NEW respiratory virus vaccine recommendations align physician groups on protection against influenza, COVID-19, and RSV. Respiratory Virus Vaccines Address a Substantial Disease Burden Four leading U.S. physician organizations have issued recommendations for the 2026–2027 respiratory virus season, covering patients from infancy through older adulthood, as well as pregnant and immunocompromised populations. The guidance followed structured reviews of vaccine safety, effectiveness, and epidemiology. Researchers examined 69 influenza studies, 155 COVID-19 studies, and 75 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) studies published between August 2025 and June 2026. More than a dozen randomized controlled trials were included for each pathogen. The recommendations arrive as respiratory viruses continue to cause substantial morbidity and mortality. During the 2025–2026 season, influenza was associated with at least 390,000 hospitalizations and 24,000 deaths. RSV caused an estimated 170,000 to 340,000 hospitalizations, while COVID-19 was linked to between 140,000 and 250,000 hospitalizations. Evidence Supports Protection Against Severe Illness Influenza vaccination reduced hospitalization risk by 31% among adults aged 65 years or older. Vaccination during pregnancy reduced symptomatic influenza among infants younger than 6 months by 44%, while pediatric influenza vaccination was associated with an 80% reduction in deaths across eight seasons. COVID-19 vaccination reduced hospitalization risk by 53% among adults aged 65 years or older. Among people with immunocompromising conditions, vaccination lowered the risk of intensive care admission or death by 32% to 53%. Vaccination during pregnancy also reduced emergency department or urgent care visits by 58%. RSV vaccines were 69% to 83% effective against hospitalization among adults aged 60 years or older. Maternal RSV vaccination reduced RSV risk by 82%, while infant immunization with nirsevimab lowered hospitalization risk by 64% to 93%. No new safety concerns were identified across the three evidence reviews. Respiratory Virus Vaccine Recommendations by Population The guidance supports annual influenza vaccination for everyone aged 6 months or older. COVID-19 vaccination recommendations vary by age and clinical status, with particular emphasis on older adults, young children, pregnant patients, healthcare personnel, and people with compromised immune systems. RSV vaccination is recommended for adults aged 50 to 74 years with high risk conditions and all adults aged 75 years or older. Preventive options for infants include maternal RSV vaccination or nirsevimab, depending on eligibility and maternal vaccination history. For clinicians, the recommendations provide an evidence based framework for vaccine counseling and shared decision making ahead of the respiratory virus season. Reference O’Reilly KB. Doctors united on respiratory virus vaccine recommendations. 2 September 2026. Article will play after ad... Playing in :00 shares Share this Article Share Share via device FacebookXLinkedInWhatsAppRedditEmailCopy Link Staff view Comments Immunization recommendations from West Coast Health Alliance has been released for the 2026-27 respiratory virus season. Acording to West Coast Health Alliance, the recommendations are informed by guidance from trusted national medical organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American Academy of Family Physicians. “As we enter the 2026-27 respiratory virus season, we recommend the recently available updated vaccine formulations to reduce the risk of severe illness,” said Hawai‘i State Epidemiologist Dr. Sarah Kemble. “We also continue to recommend other steps, such as practicing good hygiene and staying home when sick, to help people stay healthy, especially as we’re experiencing an increase in cases.” Immunization is one of the best protections available against serious illness caused by respiratory viruses such as COVID-19, influenza and respiratory syncytial virus. Seasonal immunization is also a critical public health tool to reduce serious illness and strain on health care systems. The West Coast Health Alliance believes that all recommended immunizations should be accessible to people in its member states and emphasizes the importance of protecting people most impacted by these respiratory viruses, especially those who are most vulnerable. The West Coast Health Alliance will continue to evaluate new evidence and recommendations as they become available and is committed to sharing updated assessments with communities. Specifically, West Coast Health Alliance recommends: Age/Condition COVID-19 Influenza RSV Children All 6–23 months All 2–18 years with risk factors or never vaccinated against COVID-19 All who are in close contact with others with risk factors All who choose to reduce risk of severe illness All 6 months and older All younger than 8 months All 8-19 months with risk factors Pregnancy All who are planning pregnancy, pregnant or postpartum All who are planning pregnancy, pregnant or postpartum All who are 32-36 weeks gestational age3, 4 Adults All 65 years and older All 19–64 years with risk factors All who are in close contact with others with risk factors All who choose to reduce risk of severe illness All All 75 years and older All 50–74 years with risk factors Healthcare Workers All All All who meet criteria above ADVERTISEMENT Big Island Now Staff Read Full Bio Sponsored Content View All Jobs Bowman Termite & Pest Management, LLC Fumigation Techinians Hilo · 2 weeks ago Looking for locally based talent? news.excerpt: The groups advised many people should receive vaccines against influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus.

news.content_title: Medical Groups Offer Vaccine Recommendations for Fall, Winter
news.content: Open menu NTD Television U.S.ChinaWorldPoliticsHealthBusinessEntertainmentSports More ●LIVE search EN▼ NTD Television NewsHealth News Medical Groups Offer Vaccine Recommendations for Fall, Winter The groups advised many people should receive vaccines against influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus. By Zachary Stieber | Published: 9/3/2026, 4:01:55 PM EDT A nurse practitioner holds a vaccine in a file photograph. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images) Medical groups are recommending that many people receive vaccines against respiratory viruses this fall and winter. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends COVID-19 vaccination for all children aged 6 to 23 months, as well as children aged 2 through 18 who fall in certain categories, such as being unvaccinated or living with people deemed at high risk for severe COVID-19. Other children aged 2 to 18 can receive a vaccine if their parents want them to, the academy said. The American Academy of Family Physicians is advising COVID-19 vaccinations for those same children, as well as virtually all adults. The groups are also recommending influenza vaccination for all people aged 6 months and older, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccination for pregnant women, people 75 years of age and older, and people aged 50 to 74 with certain conditions such as chronic liver disease or living in a nursing home. Also, children aged from zero to 19 months should generally receive RSV vaccination, according to the new advice, if their mother did not receive an RSV vaccine during pregnancy. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists is recommending pregnant women receive vaccines against COVID-19, flu, and RSV, as it has done before. The recommendations come ahead of the virus season, which runs through the fall and winter. The recommendations were based on effectiveness, including estimates that flu vaccines were 16 percent to 53 percent effective in late 2024 and early 2025. The organizations represent doctors and accept money or donations from vaccine manufacturers. The Department of Health and Human Services, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s parent agency, did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication. The CDC, with assistance from its vaccine advisory panel, usually updates vaccine recommendations regularly, including ahead of the virus season. In January, the CDC announced a new schedule that narrowed recommendations for COVID-19 and influenza vaccination, among others. A federal judge blocked the update, determining officials did not take proper steps before announcing it. The order has prevented the CDC’s vaccine advisers from meeting. An appeal is ongoing. The CDC website says that “because of legal uncertainties and inquiries,” its recommendations for influenza vaccines are for annual vaccination for all people aged 6 months and older, instead of the updated advice. Its page on COVID-19 vaccines has not been updated this year. Federal regulators just approved new COVID-19 vaccines without human data. The CDC would normally decide which people should receive the vaccines following new approvals, absent the court order. The CDC recommends pregnant women receive flu vaccines and RSV vaccines, but not COVID-19 vaccines. Dr. Jane Orient, executive director of the Association of American Physicians and Surgeons, which does not accept pharmaceutical funding, said that RSV vaccines are so new that there has not been enough time to assess them. Orient told The Epoch Times in an email that the influenza vaccine “is generally not very effective, and has a high incidence of adverse effects.” And she said that COVID-19 vaccines also have troubling adverse reactions, and that there are effective treatments for COVID-19, such as repurposed drugs. From The Epoch Times

The CDC has not updated its page on COVID-19 vaccines this year, and the effectiveness of flu vaccines is estimated at 16 percent to 53 percent. Some critics, like Jane Orient, have raised concerns about the safety and effectiveness of RSV vaccines, noting that they are relatively new and lack sufficient data. The CDC's recommendations for RSV vaccines are not yet updated due to the ongoing legal challenges.
news.summary_zh: Medical groups in the United States are recommending vaccines against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and COVID-19 for the fall and winter season. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children aged 6 to 23 months and those aged 2 to 18 in certain categories should receive RSV vaccines, while the CDC recommends annual flu vaccination for all people aged 6 months and older. However, the CDC has not updated its recommendations for influenza and COVID-19 vaccines this year due to legal uncertainties. A federal judge blocked an updated schedule for these vaccines in January 2026, citing insufficient procedural steps, and the CDC's vaccine advisers are unable to meet. The CDC's website states that its influenza vaccine recommendations are based on effectiveness data from late 2024 and early 2025, but the updated schedule remains unimplemented. The recommendations are made ahead of the virus season, which typically runs through the fall and winter. The CDC also recommends RSV vaccines for pregnant women, people 75 years of age and older, and those with specific health conditions. The American Academy of Family Physicians advises similar recommendations for children and adults. The CDC has not updated its page on COVID-19 vaccines this year, and the effectiveness of flu vaccines is estimated at 16 percent to 53 percent. Some critics, like Jane Orient, have raised concerns about the safety and effectiveness of RSV vaccines, noting that they are relatively new and lack sufficient data. The CDC's recommendations for RSV vaccines are not yet updated due to the ongoing legal challenges.

analysis_zh.event: 包括美国儿科学会和美国妇产科医师学会在内的医疗团体建议针对特定人群使用 疫苗,而不是 呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV)。由于法律上的不确定性,CDC 尚未更新其针对流感和 COVID-19 疫苗 的建议。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: The recommendations cover a broad population, including children, pregnant women, and elderly individuals. The CDC's influenza vaccine recommendations are for annual vaccination for all people aged 6 months and older. The effectiveness of flu vaccines is estimated at 16 percent to 53 percent. The CDC has not updated its recommendations for COVID-19 vaccines this year.
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 由于法律上的不确定性,CDC 针对流感 疫苗 的建议目前已到位。由于法院命令,CDC 的 疫苗 顾问小组无法召开会议。

news.source_body_en: The article published on September 3, 2026, by Contemporary OB/GYN discusses Kevin Ault, MD's insights on the extended RSV window in ACOG's 2026-27 immunization guidance. This guidance focuses on vaccine eligibility and does not report any confirmed outbreaks, cases, or deaths. The content is based on a full original report and is part of a broader discussion on women's health topics. No specific health-system effects or operational impacts were mentioned, and no risk level was explicitly stated. The article highlights the importance of updated recommendations for respiratory vaccines, particularly in the context of maternal and fetal health benefits. The guidance is under review and discussion, with no indication of investigation or testing related to RSV in this context.
news.content_zh: Contemporary OB/GYN 于 2026 年 9 月 3 日发表的文章讨论了医学博士 Kevin Ault 对 ACOG 2026-27 免疫指南中延长 RSV 窗口的见解。本指南重点关注 疫苗 资格,不报告任何确诊的 暴发、病例或死亡。该内容基于完整的原始报告,是有关女性健康主题的更广泛讨论的一部分。没有提及具体的卫生系统影响或运营影响,也没有明确说明风险级别。该文章强调了呼吸系统 疫苗 更新建议的重要性,特别是在孕产妇和胎儿健康益处的背景下。该指南正在审查和讨论中,没有迹象表明在这方面进行了与 RSV 相关的调查或测试。

While the review does not provide specific case counts, death numbers, or exposure data, it highlights the importance of recognizing prolonged symptoms in various respiratory viral infections. The findings are part of CIDRAP's efforts to offer evidence-based insights into respiratory illnesses, with no explicit mention of risk levels or targeted response actions. The review is based on existing data and does not include new case investigations or specific prevention measures.

news.content_title: AAP Expands RSV Vaccine Recommendations for Vulnerable Children Entering Second Season
news.content: Jump to Key Points The American Academy of Pediatrics expanded its recommendations for immunization against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) to include more children entering their second RSV season, citing evidence that certain medical conditions continue to put young children at a higher risk for severe disease. The expansion includes children aged 8 months through 19 months entering their second RSV season who have congenital heart disease, certain lung or neuromuscular conditions, or have Down syndrome or certain chromosomal conditions associated with a higher RSV risk, and those born before 32 weeks of gestation who do not need ongoing medication or support. The updated guidance for second-season immunization also includes children with certain forms of cystic fibrosis, chronic lung diseases requiring recent medical support, and all Native American and Alaska Native children. High-risk children should receive a second dose “regardless of whether their mother was immunized when they were pregnant and regardless of whether or not that infant received an RSV immunization during their first RSV season,” said Andrew Racine, MD, PhD, president of the AAP, during a press briefing announcing the recommendations. The changes reflect growing evidence that although the likelihood of hospitalization for RSV generally declines after the first year of life, some children remain at a substantially higher risk . SUGGESTED FOR YOU Children with chronic conditions affecting multiple respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal organs had more than twice the rate of hospitalizations during their second RSV season than during their first season, according to the AAP’s accompanying technical report. For infants entering their first RSV season, the AAP recommends a monoclonal antibody unless the mother received an RSV vaccine during pregnancy. RSV Season Is Lasting Longer The expanded recommendations come as other major medical organizations have updated their guidance for the 2026-2027 respiratory virus season, with some changes reflecting shifts in the timing of RSV circulation. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) extended the recommended window for the maternal RSV vaccine ABRYSVO from September 1 through March 1, rather than ending on January 31. “We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” said Christina Davidson, MD, chief medical officer at ACOG. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.” Pregnant people should receive the vaccine between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation, provided delivery is not expected within 2 weeks. If a patient does not receive the vaccine, or if the infant is born within 14 days of vaccination, the newborn should receive a monoclonal antibody for RSV. First-Season Protection Remains the Priority Despite the expansion of second-season recommendations, the AAP’s guidance emphasized protecting infants during their first RSV season. Nirsevimab reduced hospitalization risk by as much as 93% in an independent evidence review conducted by the Vaccine Integrity Project, part of the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. The AAP’s accompanying technical report found that most infants hospitalized with RSV had no underlying high-risk medical condition. Clinicians should emphasize to families that changes in RSV patterns and evolving evidence reinforce the consensus among medical organizations on the benefits of a second dose, said Sarah Nosal, MD, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong,” Nosal said. The second-dose RSV recommendations are “grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts, and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients,” Nosal said. Lara Salahi is a health journalist based in Boston. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Lingering respiratory virus symptoms aren’t limited to COVID, new review shows Laine Bergeson COVID-19 Influenza, General Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) PonyWang / iStock Share Copied to clipboard For many people who contract COVID-19, the initial infection comes with a set of worrisome symptoms, from muscle aches and fatigue to trouble breathing—and for a subset of those people, symptoms persist beyond the acute infection phase. Long COVID has become a well-known post-viral condition that can take a significant toll on health and quality of life. But SARS-CoV-2 isn’t the only virus that can have lingering aftereffects. Other respiratory viral infections (RVIs), which affect millions of people every year, can trigger persistent physical, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. A new systemic review published in Respirology examined the size and scope of persistent symptoms following non-COVID respiratory infections like influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). “Understanding post-acute sequelae of non–COVID-19 RVIs, given their global burden and relative undercharacterisation, is important to guide clinical care and public health policy,” write the researchers, who were led by a team from Duke-NUS Medical School in Singapore. Lung problems common after flu For the review, researchers analyzed 13 observational studies involving 631,863 people from January 2004 to August 2025. The flu was the most studied infection, and lung dysfunction was the most frequently reported persistent symptom. In a small 2009 study (48 participants), 54% of participants had abnormal pulmonary function 11 to 13 months after acute influenza infection. Roughly one-third reported persistent respiratory symptoms one year after infection, and over 40% reported reduced exercise tolerance. In another small study (47 participants), this one from 2017, 78% of people who survived severe flu infection had reduced ability to transfer oxygen from their lungs into their bloodstream two years later. Understanding post-acute sequelae of non–COVID-19 RVIs, given their global burden and relative undercharacterisation, is important to guide clinical care and public health policy. Findings from larger studies mirrored those from the smaller studies. Among 951 Australians diagnosed as having influenza, 23% reported symptoms after 12 weeks, and 4.4% had moderate-to-severe difficulty carrying out everyday activities. A US study of 20,844 hospitalized patients found that one in 10 still had a cough or shortness of breath six months after infection. An analysis of German insurance data from nearly 570,000 people found that 23% reported memory problems, and 44% had a distorted sense of taste or a reduced sense of smell three to six months after acute illness. Heart-related symptoms most common after RSV Two of the 13 studies in the review looked at RSV and found that cardiovascular complications were the most common persistent post-viral complaint. Among 441 US adults hospitalized with RSV, 16% experienced a heart-related event from 29 days to six months after acute infection, making the monthly rate of cardiovascular events 1.6 times higher during the post-infection period than during the six months before hospitalization. A cohort study of 1,553 adults with RSV in Singapore found that 2.1% experienced new-onset cardiac disorders after infection. The review included one small study of human metapneumovirus. Among 92 hospitalized adults, 55% reported at least one persistent symptom three to nine months after infection. Shortness of breath was most common (29%), followed by fatigue (17%), and cough (17%). The authors caution that most studies included in the review were observational and focused on hospitalized patients, making it difficult to know how often lingering symptoms occur after milder infections. They also note differences in outcome measures and follow-up approaches between the studies, concluding that future studies should use standardized definitions and outcome measures “to better define disease burden and inform targeted follow-up and prevention strategies.” Related news Previous Next Vaccine recommendations and access, plus measles deaths: 3 questions, zero consensus: The State of US Vaccine Policy Izzy Brandstetter Figueroa, PhD, MPH, Riley Mulholland, MPH, Jess Steier, DrPH Vaccine recommendations and access, plus measles deaths: 3 questions, zero consensus: The State of US Vaccine Policy Izzy Brandstetter Figueroa, PhD, MPH, Riley Mulholland, MPH, Jess Steier, DrPH COVID-19 may trigger the same immune pathway as lupus Laine Bergeson CIDRAP Op-Ed: ‘Died with, not from’ was a real COVID problem. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Lingering respiratory virus symptoms aren’t limited to COVID, new review shows Laine Bergeson COVID-19 Influenza, General Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) PonyWang / iStock Share Copied to clipboard For many people who contract COVID-19, the initial infection comes with a set of worrisome symptoms, from muscle aches and fatigue to trouble breathing—and for a subset of those people, symptoms persist beyond the acute infection phase. Long COVID has become a well-known post-viral condition that can take a significant toll on health and quality of life. But SARS-CoV-2 isn’t the only virus that can have lingering aftereffects. Other respiratory viral infections (RVIs), which affect millions of people every year, can trigger persistent physical, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. A new systemic review published in Respirology examined the size and scope of persistent symptoms following non-COVID respiratory infections like influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). “Understanding post-acute sequelae of non–COVID-19 RVIs, given their global burden and relative undercharacterisation, is important to guide clinical care and public health policy,” write the researchers, who were led by a team from Duke-NUS Medical School in Singapore. Lung problems common after flu For the review, researchers analyzed 13 observational studies involving 631,863 people from January 2004 to August 2025. The flu was the most studied infection, and lung dysfunction was the most frequently reported persistent symptom. In a small 2009 study (48 participants), 54% of participants had abnormal pulmonary function 11 to 13 months after acute influenza infection. Roughly one-third reported persistent respiratory symptoms one year after infection, and over 40% reported reduced exercise tolerance. In another small study (47 participants), this one from 2017, 78% of people who survived severe flu infection had reduced ability to transfer oxygen from their lungs into their bloodstream two years later. Understanding post-acute sequelae of non–COVID-19 RVIs, given their global burden and relative undercharacterisation, is important to guide clinical care and public health policy. Findings from larger studies mirrored those from the smaller studies. Among 951 Australians diagnosed as having influenza, 23% reported symptoms after 12 weeks, and 4.4% had moderate-to-severe difficulty carrying out everyday activities. A US study of 20,844 hospitalized patients found that one in 10 still had a cough or shortness of breath six months after infection. An analysis of German insurance data from nearly 570,000 people found that 23% reported memory problems, and 44% had a distorted sense of taste or a reduced sense of smell three to six months after acute illness. Heart-related symptoms most common after RSV Two of the 13 studies in the review looked at RSV and found that cardiovascular complications were the most common persistent post-viral complaint. Among 441 US adults hospitalized with RSV, 16% experienced a heart-related event from 29 days to six months after acute infection, making the monthly rate of cardiovascular events 1.6 times higher during the post-infection period than during the six months before hospitalization. A cohort study of 1,553 adults with RSV in Singapore found that 2.1% experienced new-onset cardiac disorders after infection. The review included one small study of human metapneumovirus. Among 92 hospitalized adults, 55% reported at least one persistent symptom three to nine months after infection. Shortness of breath was most common (29%), followed by fatigue (17%), and cough (17%). The authors caution that most studies included in the review were observational and focused on hospitalized patients, making it difficult to know how often lingering symptoms occur after milder infections. news.title_zh: 新的审查显示,挥之不去的呼吸道病毒症状不仅限于新冠病毒
news.source_body_en: A new systemic review published in Respirology examined persistent symptoms following non-COVID respiratory infections, including influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The review analyzed 13 observational studies involving 631,863 people from January 2004 to August 2025, highlighting that lung dysfunction, fatigue, and other symptoms can linger after infection. For RSV, cardiovascular complications were the most common persistent post-viral complaint, with 16% of hospitalized adults experiencing heart-related events within 29 days to six months post-infection. Persistent symptoms were also reported in 23% of flu patients and 55% of those with human metapneumovirus. The authors caution that most studies were observational and focused on hospitalized patients, making it difficult to know how often lingering symptoms occur after milder infections. They emphasize the need for standardized definitions and outcome measures to better define disease burden and inform targeted follow-up and prevention strategies.
news.content_zh: 《呼吸学》杂志上发表的一项新的系统综述检查了非新冠肺炎呼吸道感染后的持续症状,包括流感和 呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV)。该综述分析了 2004 年 1 月至 2025 年 8 月期间涉及 631,863 人的 13 项观察性研究,强调肺功能障碍、疲劳和其他症状可能在感染后持续存在。对于 RSV,心血管并发症是最常见的持续性病毒感染后症状,16% 的住院成人在感染后 29 天至 6 个月内出现心脏相关事件。23% 的流感患者和 55% 的人类偏肺病毒患者也报告有持续症状。作者警告说,大多数研究都是观察性的,并且集中于住院患者,因此很难知道较轻微的感染后持续出现症状的频率。他们强调需要标准化的定义和结果测量,以更好地定义疾病负担并为有针对性的后续行动和预防策略提供信息。

news.content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local Weather Video Investigations Entertainment Sports NBC 5 Responds Newsletters Fair 82o Watch 24/7 Create profile / Log in Dashboard Email preferences Sign out Trending 24/7 Streaming News Chicago Sports Must-See Videos Chicago Today Matt in the Morning Open House Chicago Roeper's Reviews Expand 1 Weather Alert Health & Wellness Fall vaccines: Latest Covid, flu RSV vaccine recommendations as some cases rise In Illinois, the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that COVID cases are already trending upwards. By NBC Chicago Staff and The Associated Press • Published September 3, 2026 • Updated on September 3, 2026 at 11:54 am Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER A Walgreens sign advertising free flu shots is seen outside a store in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on August 9, 2026. (Photo by Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Leading U.S. medical groups are urging people to get updated flu and COVID-19 vaccinations this fall, banding together Wednesday to issue shot guidelines — and highlight the science behind them — saying they hope to ease confusion caused by the Trump administration’s changing advice. Flu vaccinations are beginning and COVID-19 shots are starting to arrive after the Food and Drug Administration approved this year’s updated versions last week. Winter also brings another vaccine-preventable risk called RSV. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE In Illinois, the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that COVID cases are already trending upwards. The trend is the same for 47 other states, with the CDC saying the respiratory virus is "likely growing." But who should get one or all of these vaccines, and when? That advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with help from its independent advisers. But despite no new scientific evidence, Trump health officials last year began pulling back on some longstanding recommendations for fall virus protection and routine children’s vaccinations. And that advisory panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle. The CDC didn’t respond to questions about any new fall guidance but suggested on its website that doctors follow last year’s flu recommendations. Doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America each released vaccination guidelines for their patient populations. Local Frankfort 15 minutes ago Frankfort mom accused of killing son said she intended to kill other kids, husband: Pros. chicago concerts 51 minutes ago Stevie Wonder's ‘Songs in the Key of Life' tour features Chicago show “There’s been a lot of confusion and chaos regarding vaccine recommendations,” said Dr. Sandra Fryhofer, of the American Medical Association. All the groups’ recommendations plus evidence on shot safety and effectiveness are being posted on websites so “the public has clear, consistent, science-based guidance even while the federal process is in flux,” Fryhofer said. Who should get the flu shot? Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons were especially harsh, with unusually high numbers of child deaths — the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids. The vaccines don’t block all flu infections but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults’ hospitalizations by 31%, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota. Its analysis was published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA. Three “enhanced” flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — “but do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available,” said AAFP’s Dr. Sarah Nosal. There’s a new choice this year for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna’s mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot. The FDA just approved the new option and the company expects some doses to be available soon at certain pharmacies. The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they’re ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria. Flu shots are currently widely available at pharmacies like Walgreens and CVS. They are also offered in some doctors and pediatricians offices. Who can and should get the COVID vaccine? Earlier this month, the FDA approved Pfizer and BioNTech's updated COVID shot for 2026-27 targeting the XFG variant. COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk. Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it. With millions of shots administered, there’s no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, “so please get the vaccine,” said ACOG’s Dr. Christina Davidson. Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi. Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children. Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots. Where you can get the COVID shot For COVID-19 shots, states have more pharmacy rules. COVID-19 tends to rise in late summer, as it is now, and again after the winter holidays. The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems. It’s also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren’t vaccinated and some other high-risk babies. (Photo by Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Leading U.S. medical groups are urging people to get updated flu and COVID-19 vaccinations this fall, banding together Wednesday to issue shot guidelines — and highlight the science behind them — saying they hope to ease confusion caused by the Trump administration’s changing advice. Flu vaccinations are beginning and COVID-19 shots are starting to arrive after the Food and Drug Administration approved this year’s updated versions last week. Winter also brings another vaccine-preventable risk called RSV. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE In Illinois, the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that COVID cases are already trending upwards. The trend is the same for 47 other states, with the CDC saying the respiratory virus is "likely growing." But who should get one or all of these vaccines, and when? That advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with help from its independent advisers. But despite no new scientific evidence, Trump health officials last year began pulling back on some longstanding recommendations for fall virus protection and routine children’s vaccinations. And that advisory panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle. The CDC didn’t respond to questions about any new fall guidance but suggested on its website that doctors follow last year’s flu recommendations. Doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America each released vaccination guidelines for their patient populations. Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children.
