news.content: Ephrem Chen, 9, receives a COVID-19 booster shot and a flu vaccine from an IDPH nurse during a walk-in clinic on Dec. 3, 2023, at St. Procopius School in Pilsen. Illinois is recommending the COVID-19 vaccine this respiratory virus season for all children ages 6 to 23 months old and for children between the ages of 2 and 17 if they are in higher risk groups, or if their parents want them to have the shot, recommendations that are similar to those made by the American Academy of Pediatrics. (Brian Cassella/Chicago Tribune) By Charles Selle | For the Lake County News-Sun PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 2:29 PM CDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Some parents must have been on the fence when it came to ensuring their children were vaccinated before beginning new-school-year classes last month. At least in Douglas County along the Interstate 57 corridor. That’s one conclusion coming from the measles outbreak in the east-central Illinois county which is home to the burgs of Tuscola and Arcola. Four confirmed cases of the disease have been reported in the county by the state’s Department of Public Health despite some 98% of school-age children there being vaccinated. If that’s the case, it seems our vaccination policies need a shot in the arm to get to the 100% mark. Or we need to start getting straight talk about vaccines from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Most folks understand that vaccines are modern medical miracles. With immunizations, parents no longer have to be concerned about their children contracting childhood diseases such as polio, tetanus and chickenpox. Smallpox was a feared cause of death in the U.S. Since 1977, it has been declared eliminated. The World Health Organization estimates vaccines prevent around 3.5 million to 5 million deaths per year across the globe. Despite those in some quarters questioning the use of vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, serums manufactured and distributed during the outbreak saved millions of Americans and more at a time when millions were dying after being infected with the coronavirus. Highly contagious measles was considered eradicated in the U.S. in 2000. But increasing doubts about vaccines and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s insistence that shots are unsafe has led to an uptick in cases of measles across the nation. Health officials in Illinois and other states continue to preach vaccine safety, especially when it comes to measles and other diseases considered in the childhood category. Yet, this year there have been nine cases of measles in Illinois, including one in Kane County, according to a recent Chicago Tribune story. Last year, the state had 14 cases of measles. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said there have so far been nearly 3,000 confirmed cases of measles in the nation, the largest number in a decade. Of those cases, some 94% were in unvaccinated people, according to the CDC. Nationally, Utah has had 526 cases this year, and South Carolina has had 670, the CDC reports. Illinois has a high rate of vaccinations among its populace, state officials say. Yet, we remain in 27th place among all states, just below New Mexico and just above North Carolina, according to one health study. Vermont is the highest-vaxxed state in the nation; Mississippi the worst. Illinois requires all school-age children to be immunized against a bunch of diseases — among them diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, polio, rubella, mumps and measles — before enrolling in school. State health officials support the American Academy of Pediatrics’ vaccination schedule. Meanwhile, the Chicago-based American Medical Association continues to urge adults, especially seniors, to be vaccinated for a variety of ailments. Our immune systems weaken over time, medical professionals say, and keeping up to date with vaccines becomes even more important as we age. Considered necessary immunizations by the CDC include seasonal flu shots, current COVID-19 vaccines and shingles jabs. Also, vaccines for RSV, a respiratory disease, pneumonia, tetanus boosters and Hepatitis B infections. Health Secretary Kennedy, 72, a lawyer and determined anti-vaccine advocate, has questioned the efficacy of a number of those immunizations and has attempted to strong-arm changes to national vaccine policy, according to several reports. He has challenged the safety of shots for common diseases, like measles, contended COVID-19 serums were dangerous, and theorized that many vaccines have not been properly tested and can cause a range of dangerous side effects. During his term, he has ended development of mRNA vaccines, withdrawn funding for an international vaccine alliance, and narrowed access to COVID-19 shots. His views run counter to medical professionals and scientists who maintain the secretary seeds fear among Americans when it comes to the safety of immunizations. Especially parents. Millions and millions of Americans have received a litany of immunizations over decades of medical care. The facts are that these diseases have been stamped out through the use of vaccines. Diseases which once shortened the lifespans of Americans continue to be afterthoughts. There’s no reason to change research policies. Solid science backs the outcomes of vaccines. Charles Selle is a former News-Sun reporter, political editor, and editor. sellenews@gmail.com. GPB’s Sofi Gratas has more. Credit: Adobe Stock A group of independent medical associations is issuing its own vaccine recommendations ahead of respiratory virus season, apart from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Respiratory virus season usually lasts from fall through mid-Spring, with cases of common infectious diseases spiking in the winter. It’s the second year since the overhaul of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices that guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Family Physicians and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have been released independent from the federal government. The groups are in collaboration with the Vaccine Integrity Project housed at the University of Minnesota. In years past, the groups were aligned with the federal agency, said Dr. Bruce Gellin of the Vaccine Integrity Project on a press call Tuesday. “Unfortunately, today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that historically has,” he said. “But the need for that work has not disappeared.” Last year, the ACIP indicated it intended to stray from the traditionally recommended vaccine schedule and instead encourage “shared clinical decision-making" for several childhood vaccines. Members also considered removing a universal recommendation that newborns get vaccinated against Hepatitis B. But now, ahead of the expected spike in flu, COVID, and RSV, the ACIP can’t meet or issue guidance on vaccines until the court decides if President Trump’s overhaul of the committee was illegal. RELATED: Federal judge pauses changes made by the CDC's vaccine advisory committee The CDC extended its 2025 recommendations for the upcoming respiratory virus season this week. Reported vaccination rates this year among school-aged children remain below pre-pandemic levels, with the rate of vaccine exemptions filed in Georgia schools on a steady uptick. Georgia’s Department of Public Health is supportive of the recommendations from medical groups and those made by the CDC “for many years,” confirmed agency spokesperson Nancy Nydam Shirek. It also supports the key principle of “shared clinical decision-making.” “DPH continues to urge parents to consult with their healthcare provider to determine what best meets their child’s medical needs and to ask questions they may have about vaccines and the diseases they prevent,” Nydam Shirek wrote. Local public health departments across the state offer vaccines for adults and children, regardless of insurance status. Guidance important for months to follow All recommendations from the participating organizations, in collaboration with the Vaccine Integrity Project, come with an evidence review, each published in JAMA, Dr. Ronald Nahass with the Infectious Diseases Society of America told the press. “I think the point is to make sure that the medical community, which we're here representing that, is uniform in our effort to bring clarity and to restore that trust,” Nahass said. Last fall and winter, Georgia saw a five-year high for flu deaths with over 200 reported, and an extended RSV season. Both viruses can be more serious in older adults and kids. The flu vaccine is 40-60% effective in preventing serious illness that could result in hospitalization. It’s widely recommended for everyone over six months old. A vaccine to protect against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is at this point recommended as a one-time dose. Symptoms mimic the common cold but can cause severe complications in older adults and immunocompromised people. Babies, too, can be hospitalized with RSV, particularly if it morphs into a lower respiratory infection, said Dr. Robert Wiskind, a practicing physician and representative for the Georgia chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. He recommends infants get a dose in their first year, unless mothers are vaccinated while pregnant. That's in line with the national organization's guidelines this year. “It’s been remarkably successful,” he said. “And it's safe, and it is only one dose that lasts throughout the five to six-month respiratory season.” The AAP also recommends an annual, updated COVID vaccine for almost everyone, even as spikes in viral infection have been less severe. “It is true that a lot of people who get COVID now have a milder case, probably because they have immunity from previous illnesses or previous vaccination,” Wiskind said. “But it's also true that COVID-19 can still be a significant illness for adults, for children, especially young children or children with other health conditions.” Last year, access to COVID vaccines for many was thrown into question when the federal Food and Drug Administration placed restrictions on who was eligible for the updated vaccines, under the direction of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. news.content_title: Dealroom.co | Clover posts positive Phase 2 data for its combination respiratory vaccines in older adults
news.content: Clover Biopharmaceuticals reported positive preliminary results on 6 September 2026 from a mid-stage (Phase 2) trial of two experimental vaccines designed to protect older adults against several respiratory viruses at once. The results matter because they push Clover closer to competing in the fast-growing market for shots that guard against multiple winter respiratory infections in one dose. The trial, run in Australia in 420 adults aged 60 to 85, tested two candidates: SCB-1022, which targets RSV (respiratory syncytial virus, a common cause of serious lung infections in the elderly) and hMPV (human metapneumovirus, a related respiratory bug), and SCB-1033, which adds protection against a third virus, PIV3 (parainfluenza type 3). Both are protein-based vaccines built on Clover's Trimer-Tag platform, the company's own technology for assembling vaccine ingredients. Twenty-eight days after vaccination, both shots triggered strong immune responses — roughly a 6-to-9-fold rise in virus-fighting antibodies against RSV and 6-to-8-fold against hMPV — with no fall-off in the oldest participants (75+). Adding the third virus target did not weaken the response to the other two. Vaccinated groups also saw about 62% fewer respiratory infections than placebo during a local RSV outbreak, and the shots were generally well tolerated with no vaccine-related serious side effects. Clover is positioning the vaccines partly as a booster for people who have already had an approved RSV shot, and says the data — plus a successful commercial-scale manufacturing run — lowers the risk of moving into larger late-stage trials. The company plans to advance both candidates and seek global partners. Source: Clover Biopharmaceuticals, 6 September 2026

news.content_zh: Clover Biopharmaceuticals 于 2026 年 9 月 6 日报告了两种实验性联合呼吸系统 疫苗 的 2 期试验的积极初步结果。该试验在澳大利亚进行,受试者为 420 名 60 至 85 岁的成年人,测试了针对 RSV (呼吸道合胞病毒) 和 hMPV(人类偏肺病毒)的 疫苗,第三种候选药物还包括针对 PIV3(副流感病毒)的保护类型 3)。两种 疫苗 都触发了强烈的 免疫应答,针对 RSV 的抗体增加了 6 至 9 倍,针对 hMPV 的抗体增加了 6 至 8 倍,并且最年长的参与者(75 岁以上)没有下降。在 RSV 暴发 期间,接种疫苗组的呼吸道感染比安慰剂组减少了约 62%。疫苗 的耐受性良好,没有严重的副作用。Clover 正在推进这两种候选药物并寻求全球合作伙伴,并引用数据和成功的制造来降低进入更大规模试验的风险。这些调查结果是初步的,需要进一步调查。

Scrip >>Disease >>Anti-infective China Approves Global-First Nine-Month Prophylactic Antibody For Infant RSV Sep 04 2026 • By Xu Hu • 2 min read SummaryGenerate a summary of this article Download Translate Bookmark Listen to this article Trinomab’s global-first long-acting prophylactic antibody provides nine months of protection for newborns and infants entering their first respiratory syncytial virus season. Greater efficacy was seen in those at high risk of infection. Chinese approval for world-first homegrown antibody for RSV (Shutterstock) China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has granted the world’s first approval for a monoclonal antibody for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prophylaxis that provides nine-month protection for newborns and infants, including full-term and late preterm infants and those at high risk of RSV infection, who are entering or born during the first RSV season. Key Takeaways China has approved the world’s first prophylactic antibody to provide nine-month protection for newborns and infants entering or born during their first respiratory syncytial virus season - Trinomab's retavibart. The drug retavibart targets the prefusion protein of RSV and was developed by Zhuhai-headquartered Trinomab Pharmaceutical. analysis.time: China approved the nine-month prophylactic antibody for infant RSV on Sep 04 2026, with the event date being the first RSV season for newborns and infants.
analysis.location_and_population: China, targeting newborns and infants, including full-term and late preterm infants, and those at high risk of RSV infection.
analysis.event: China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) approved the world’s first monoclonal antibody for RSV prophylaxis that provides nine-month protection for newborns and infants entering their first RSV season. This is a confirmed event based on official approval.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The drug, retavibart, provides nine months of protection for infants at high risk of RSV infection, showing greater efficacy in these groups. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The approval is confirmed, and the drug is now available for use in China. The response status is active, with no unresolved information or limitations mentioned in the evidence.

analysis.brief_en: China has approved the world’s first nine-month prophylactic antibody for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in newborns and infants, marking a significant advancement in pediatric healthcare. The drug, retavibart, developed by Trinomab Pharmaceutical, targets the prefusion protein of RSV and is designed to protect infants during their first RSV season. This approval is confirmed by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) and is intended for full-term and late preterm infants, as well as those at high risk of infection. The evidence highlights that greater efficacy was observed in high-risk groups, though no specific case counts or death numbers are provided. The response status is active, with the drug now available for use in China. This development could reshape RSV prevention strategies for vulnerable infants.

(WDBJ) - An independent fall vaccine review from the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project was published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA. It is helping to guide recommendations from several U.S. medical groups, including the American Academy of Family Physicians. Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said the goal is to provide clear guidance. “We’re gonna bring you, bring you the strongest, safest recommendations to keep your family healthy, just like you’re prioritizing,” Nosal said. Flu vaccine recommendations Beginning in October, everyone six months and older is advised to get an annual flu shot. People who are pregnant should also receive the flu vaccine, but should avoid the nasal spray version. Adults 65 and older should receive an enhanced vaccine, if it’s available. Adults 50 and older are approved to get the new mRNA-based flu vaccine. RSV vaccine recommendations For RSV, now through early fall, adults 75 and older, and those ages 50 to 74 at higher risk of severe illness, should receive a one-time RSV vaccine. The RSV vaccine is also recommended for people who are immunocompromised, those 32 to 36 weeks pregnant between September 1 and March 1, and infants under eight months who didn’t receive maternal protection. Children up to 19 months of age at high risk of severe RSV disease are advised to receive one of two FDA-approved monoclonal antibodies for protection. COVID-19 vaccine recommendations It is currently recommended that all adults 19 years and older who haven’t had a recent COVID-19 infection receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine. This also applies to infants between six and 23 months and children in certain high-risk groups. “This is the potential and ability to both protect ourselves from severe illness and protect the people around us from spreading infection,” Nosal said. Ongoing impact of respiratory viruses The Vaccine Integrity Project says the burden of respiratory viruses has changed since the COVID-19 pandemic. Influenza, RSV and COVID-19 continue to send hundreds of thousands of people to U.S. hospitals and lead to tens of thousands of deaths every year. Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved. analysis.brief_en: The article outlines vaccine recommendations for flu, RSV, and COVID-19 from a family medicine physician, emphasizing the importance of vaccination to protect individuals and communities. Published on September 4, 2026, in Roanoke, Virginia, the recommendations are based on an independent review by the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project, which was published in the medical journal JAMA. These findings are guiding several U.S. medical groups, including the American Academy of Family Physicians, in providing clear guidance.
